entries.6527a02c36467d20070c9da5e6e575de99211c6f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen16261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16262" type="x-p"/> If I justify myself - God must have some reason for his conduct towards me; I therefore do not pretend to justify myself; the attempt to do it would be an insult to his majesty and justice. Though I am conscious of none of the crimes of which you accuse me; and know not why he contends with me; yet he must have some reason, and that reason he does not choose to explain.
entries.d9103fa58d0d5f7a46b7ff5ba87156b6a3063ba5: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen16262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16263" type="x-p"/> Though I were perfect - Had I the fullest conviction that, in every thought, word, and deed, I were blameless before him, yet I would not plead this; nor would I think it any security for a life of ease and prosperity, or any proof that my days should be prolonged.
entries.fa8d464aac4fcad39a50dae1052eb7c5e9b44a01: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen16263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16264" type="x-p"/> This is one thing - My own observation shows, that in the course of providence the righteous and the wicked have an equal lot; for when any sudden calamity comes, the innocent and the guilty fall alike. There may be a few exceptions, but they are very extraordinary, and very rare.
entries.63d8c81a32ef59c84a6a3f6c8723f233364ed84f: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen16264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16265" type="x-p"/> The earth is given into the hand of the wicked - Is it not most evident that the worst men possess most of this world's goods, and that the righteous are scarcely ever in power or affluence? This was the case in Job's time; it is the case still. Therefore prosperity and adversity in this life are no marks either of God's approbation or disapprobation. <div eID="gen16265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16266" type="x-p"/> He covereth the faces of the judges thereon - Or, The faces of its decisions he shall cover. God is often stated in Scripture as doing a thing which he only permits to be done. So he permits the eyes of judgment to be blinded; and hence false decisions. Mr. Good translates the verse thus: - "The earth is given over to the hand of Injustice; <div eID="gen16266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16267" type="x-p"/> She hoodwinketh the faces of its judges. <div eID="gen16267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16268" type="x-p"/> Where every one liveth is it not so?" <div eID="gen16268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16269" type="x-p"/> And vindicates the translation in his learned notes: but I think the Hebrew will not bear this rendering; especially that in the third line. <div eID="gen16269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16270" type="x-p"/> Where, and who is he? - If this be not the case, who is he that acts in this way, and where is he to be found? If God does not permit these things, who is it that orders them? Coverdale translates, As for the worlde, he geveth it over into the power of the wicked, such as the rulers be wherof all londes are full. Is it not so? Where is there eny, but he is soch one? This sense is clear enough, if the original will bear it. The last clause is thus rendered by the Syriac and Arabic, Who can bear his indignation?
entries.29b8df10cec442eeff1e0cd7f004c1f2014d9bcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen16270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16271" type="x-p"/> Swifter than a post - מני רץ minni rats, than a runner. The light-footed messenger or courier who carries messages from place to place. They flee away - The Chaldee says, My days are swifter than the shadow of a flying bird. So swiftly do they flee away that I cannot discern them; and when past they cannot be recalled. There is a sentiment like this in Virgil, Geor. lib. iii., ver. 284: - <div eID="gen16271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16272" type="x-p"/> Sed Fugit interea, Cubit Irreparabile tempus! - "But in the meanwhile time flies! irreparable time flies away!"
entries.910ba1e617fef61e59d17001380065839f3f6663: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen16272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16273" type="x-p"/> As the swift ships - אניות אבה oniyoth ebeh. Ships of desire, or ships of Ebeh, says our margin; perhaps more correctly, inflated ships, the sails bellying out with a fair brisk wind, tide favorable, and the vessels themselves lightly freighted. The Vulgate has, Like ships freighted with apples. Ships laden with the best fruits - Targum. Ships well adapted for sailing - Arabic. Shipes that be good under sale - Coverdale. Probably this relates to the light fast-sailing ships on the Nile, which were made of reeds or papyrus. Perhaps the idea to be seized is not so much the swiftness of the passage, as their leaving no trace or track behind them. But instead of אבה ebeh, איבה eybah, hostile ships or the ships of enemies, is the reading of forty-seven of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., and of the Syriac version. If this be the true reading what is its sense? My days are gone off like the light vessels of the pirates, having stripped me of my property, and carried all irrecoverably away, under the strongest press of sail, that they may effect their escape, and secure their booty. The next words, As the eagle that hasteth to the prey, seem at least to countenance, if not confirm, the above reading: the idea of robbery and spoil, prompt attack and sudden retreat, is preserved in both images.
entries.e17af656370e9ba305eba4c51387ba776953d32d: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen16273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16274" type="x-p"/> I will forget my complaint - I will forsake or forego my complaining. I will leave off my heaviness. Vulgate, I will change my countenance - force myself to smile, and endeavor to assume the appearance of comfort.
entries.f9af649009f3852f92728eab168649899c8b9d0e: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen16274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16275" type="x-p"/> I am afraid of all my sorrows - Coverdale translates, after the Vulgate, Then am I afrayed of all my workes. Even were I to cease from complaining, I fear lest not one of my works, however well intentioned, would stand thy scrutiny, or meet with thy approbation. <div eID="gen16275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16276" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt not hold me innocent - Coverdale, after the Vulgate, For I knowe thou favourest not an evil doer; but this is not the sense of the original: Thou wilt not acquit me so as to take away my afflictions from me.
entries.bab6d592b523f2d0ed86287975a81d272a92e163: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen16276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16277" type="x-p"/> If I be wicked - If I am the sinner you suppose me to be, in vain should I labor to counterfeit joy, and cease to complain of my sufferings.
entries.be708bf2bcfef8220fcdbf789c4fe25671726cf5: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen16277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16278" type="x-p"/> If I wash myself with snow water - Supposed to have a more detergent quality than common water; and it was certainly preferred to common water by the ancients. Of this we find an example in an elegant but licentious author: Tandem ergo discubuimus, pueris Alexandrinis Aquam in manus Nivatam infundentibus, aliisque insequentibus ad pedes - Petr. Satyr., cap. xxxi. "At length we sat down, and had snow water poured on our hands by lads of Alexandria," etc. Mr. Good supposes that there is an allusion here to the ancient rite of washing the hands in token of innocence. See <reference osisRef="Psa.26.6">Psa 26:6</reference> : I will Wash my hands in Innocency; and <reference osisRef="Psa.73.13">Psa 73:13</reference> : Verily I have cleansed my heart in vain, and Washed my Hands in Innocency. And by this ceremony Pilate declared himself innocent of the blood of Christ, <reference osisRef="Mat.27.24">Mat 27:24</reference>.
entries.826bff1b3077b24b6a2d1ca7efbf5d6233d1e081: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen16278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16279" type="x-p"/> And mine own clothes shall abhor me - Such is thine infinite purity, when put in opposition to the purity of man, that it will bear no comparison. Searched and tried by the eye of God, I should be found as a leper, so that my own clothes would dread to touch me, for fear of being infected by my corruption. This is a strong and bold figure; and is derived from the corrupted state of his body, which his clothes dreaded to touch, because of the contagious nature of his disorder.
entries.c79d6d1797ef1dfa80161a05d689bae42b212990: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen16279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16280" type="x-p"/> For he is not a man as I am - I cannot contend with him as with one of my fellows in a court of justice.
entries.9c51a61e98ae0e20953b34b0f65248c29de57fe1: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen16280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16281" type="x-p"/> Neither is there any day's-man - בינינו מוכיח beyneynu mochiach, a reprover, arguer, or umpire between us. Day's - Man, in our law, means an arbitrator, or umpire between party and party; as it were bestowing a day, or certain time on a certain day, to decree, judge, or decide a matter - Minshieu. Day is used in law for the day of appearance in court, either originally or upon assignation, for hearing a matter for trial - Idem. But arbitrator is the proper meaning of the term here: one who is, by the consent of both parties, to judge between them, and settle their differences. Instead of לא יש lo yesh, there is not, fifteen of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., with the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic, read לו יש lu vesh, I wish there were: or, O that there were! Ειθε ην ὁ μεσιτης ἡμων, και ελεγχων και διακουων αναμεσον αμφοτερων; O that we had a mediator, an advocate, and judge between us both! - Sept. Poor Job! He did not yet know the Mediator between God and man: the only means by which God and man can be brought together and reconciled. Had St. Paul this in his eye when he wrote <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.5">1Tim 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.6">1Tim 2:6</reference>? For there is one God, and one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; who gave himself a ransom for all. Without this Mediator, and the ransom price which he has laid down, God and man can never be united: and that this union might be made possible, Jesus took the human into conjunction with his Divine nature; and thus God was manifest in the flesh.
entries.42bfd5800ac0ae9caecff4ce0f96bc24c8021d0b: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen16281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16282" type="x-p"/> Let him take his rod away - In the Masoretic Bibles, the word שבטו shibto, his rod, is written with a large ט teth, as above; and as the letter in numerals stands for 9, the Masora says the word was thus written to show the nine calamities under which Job had suffered, and which he wished God to remove. As שבט shebet signifies, not only rod, but also scepter or the ensign of royalty, Job might here refer to God sitting in his majesty upon the judgment-seat; and this sight so appalled him, that, filled with terror, he was unable to speak. When a sinful soul sees God in his majesty, terror seizes upon it, and prayer is impossible. We have a beautiful illustration of this, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.1-Isa.6.5">Isa 6:1-5</reference> : "I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple. Then said I, Wo is me, for I am undone, because I am a man of unclean lips; for mine eyes have seen the King, the Lord of hosts."
entries.6ccd49247ff1221dc7af079817e64589bef8fd08: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen16282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16283" type="x-p"/> But it is not so with me - I am not in such circumstances as to plead with my Judge. I believe the sense of these words is nearly as Coverdale has expressed it: - For as longe as I am in soch fearfulnesse, I can make no answere. A natural picture of the state of a penitent soul, which needs no additional coloring. <div eID="gen16283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16284" type="x-p"/> On the names of the constellations mentioned <reference osisRef="Job.9.9">Job 9:9</reference>, and again <reference osisRef="Job.38.31">Job 38:31</reference>, etc., much has been written, and to little effect. I have already, in the notes, expressed my doubts whether any constellation be intended. Dr. Hales, however, finds in these names, as he thinks, astronomical data, by which he ascertains the time of Job. I shall give his words: - "The cardinal constellations of spring and autumn, in Job's time, were Chimah, and Chesil or Taurus, and Scorpio; noticed <reference osisRef="Job.9.9">Job 9:9</reference>, and again, <reference osisRef="Job.38.31">Job 38:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.38.32">Job 38:32</reference>; of which the principal stars are, Aldebaran, the bull's eye, and Antares, the scorpion's heart. Knowing, therefore, the longitudes of these stars, at present, the interval of time from thence to the assumed date of Job's trial will give the difference of the longitudes; and ascertain their positions then, with respect to the vernal and autumnal points of intersection of the equinoctial and ecliptic; according to the usual rate of the precession of the equinoxes, one degree in 71 years. See that article, vol. i. p. 185. "The following calculations I owe to the kindness and skill of the respectable Dr. Brinkley, Andrew's Professor of Astronomy in the University of Dublin. "In a.d. 1800 Aldebaran was in 2 signs, 7 degrees, east longitude. But since the date of Job's trial, b.c. 2338, i.e., 4138 years, the precession of the equinoxes amounted to 1 sign, 27 degrees, 53 minutes; which, being subtracted from the former quantity, left Aldebaran in only 9 degrees, 7 minutes longitude, or distance from the vernal intersection; which, falling within the constellation Taurus, consequently rendered it the cardinal constellation of spring, as Pisces is at present. "In a.d. 1800 Antares was in 8 signs, 6 degrees, 58 minutes, east longitude; or 2 signs, 6 degrees, 58 minutes, east of the autumnal intersection: from which subtracting as before the amount of the precession, Antares was left only 9 degrees, 5 minutes east. Since then, the autumnal equinox was found within Scorpio, this was the cardinal constellation of autumn, as Virgo is at present. "Such a combination and coincidence of various rays of evidence, derived from widely different sources, history, sacred and profane, chronology, and astronomy, and all converging to the same focus, tend strongly to establish the time of Job's trial, as rightly assigned to the year b.c. 2337, or 818 years after the deluge, 184 years before the birth of Abram; 474 years before the settlement of Jacob's family in Egypt; and 689 years before their exode or departure from thence." New Analysis of Chronology, vol. ii., p. 57. <div eID="gen16284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16285" type="x-p"/> Now all this is specious; and, were the foundation sound, we might rely on the permanence of the building, though the rains should descend, the floods come, and the winds blow and beat on that house. But all these deductions and conclusions are founded on the assumption that Chimah and Chesil mean Taurus and Scorpio: but this is the very point that is to be proved; for proof of this is not offered, nor, indeed, can be offered; and such assumptions are palpably nugatory. That עש ash has been generally understood to signify the Great Bear; כסיל Kesil, Orion; and כימה Kimah, the Pleiades; may be seen everywhere: but that they do signify these constellations is perfectly uncertain. We have only conjectures concerning their meaning; and on such conjectures no system can be built. Genuine data, in Dr. Hales's hands, are sure to be conducted to legitimate conclusions: but neither he nor any one else can construct an astronomical fabric in the limbus of conjecture. When Job lived is perfectly uncertain: but that this book was written 818 years after the deluge; 184 years before the birth of Abram, and 689 years before the exodus; and that all this is demonstrable from Chimah and Chesil signifying Taurus and Scorpio, whence the positions of the equinoxes at the time of Job's trial can be ascertained; can never be proved, and should never be credited. In what many learned men have written on this subject, I find as much solidity and satisfaction as from what is piously and gravely stated in the Glossa Ordinaria: - <div eID="gen16285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16286" type="x-p"/> Qui facit Arcturum. Diversae sunt constellationes, varios status ecclesiae signantes. Per Arcturum, qui semper super orizontem nostrum apparet, significatur status apostolorum qui in episcopis remanet. Per Oriona, qui est tempestatis signum, significatur status martyrum. Per Hyadas, quae significant pluvios, status doctorum doctrinae pluvium effundentium. Per interiora austri, quae sunt nobis occulta, status Anachoretarum, hominum aspectus declinantium. "These different constellations signify various states of the Church. By Arcturus, which always appears above our horizon, is signified the apostolic state, which still remains in episcopacy. By Orion, which is a tempestuous sign, is signified the state of the martyrs. By the Hyades, (kids), which indicate rain, the state of the doctors, pouring out the rain of doctrine, is signified. And by the inner chambers of the south, which are hidden from us, the state of the Anchorets (hermits) is signified, who always shun the sight of men." <div eID="gen16286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16287" type="x-p"/> Much more of the same allegorical matter may be found in the same place, the Glossa Ordinaria of Strabus of Fulda, on the ninth chapter of Job. But how unreal and empty are all these things! What an uncertain sound do such trumpets give!  <chapter eID="Job.9"/> <div eID="gen16287" type="x-p"/>

entries.bc221c64fbfedd9636fb601f4f2253e4f200f909: <reference osisRef="Job.9.1-Job.4.1">Job 9:1-4   1</reference>  Then Job began, and said:   2  Yea, indeed, I know it is thus, <div eID="gen7175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7176" type="x-p"/> And how should a man be just with God!   3  Should he wish to contend with God, <div eID="gen7176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7177" type="x-p"/> He could not answer Him one of a thousand.   4  The wise in heart and mighty in strength, <div eID="gen7177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7178" type="x-p"/> Who hath defied Him and remained unhurt? <div eID="gen7178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7179" type="x-p"/> Job does not (<reference osisRef="Job.9.1">Job 9:1</reference>) refer to what Eliphaz said (<reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference>), which is similar, though still not exactly the same; but “indeed I know it is so” must be supposed to be an assert to that which Bildad had said immediately before. The chief thought of Bildad’s speech was, that God does not pervert what is right. Certainly (אמנם, <hi type="italic">scilicet</hi>, <hi type="italic">nimirum</hi>, like <reference osisRef="Job.12.2">Job 12:2</reference>), - says Job, as he ironically confirms this maxim of Bildad’s, - it is so: what God does is always right, because God does it; how could man maintain that he is in the right in opposition to God! If God should be willing to enter into controversy with man, he would not be able to give Him information on one of a thousand subjects that might be brought into discussion; he would be so confounded, so disarmed, by reason of the infinite distance of the feeble creature from his Creator. The attributes (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.9.4">Job 9:4</reference></hi>) belong not to man (Olshausen), but to God, as Job 36:5. God is wise of heart (לב = νοῦς) in putting one question after another, and mighty in strength in bringing to nought every attempt man may make to maintain his own right; to defy Him (הקשׁה, to harden, i.e., ערף, the neck), therefore, always tends to the discomfiture of him who dares to bid Him defiance.
entries.01ec07ab037c128261f74f1cf1c6167994183934: <reference osisRef="Job.9.5-Job.7.5">Job 9:5-7   5</reference>  Who removeth mountains without their knowing, <div eID="gen7179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7180" type="x-p"/> That He hath overturned them in His wrath;   6  Who causeth the earth to shake out of its place, <div eID="gen7180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7181" type="x-p"/> And its pillars to tremble;   7  Who commandeth the sun, and it riseth not, <div eID="gen7181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7182" type="x-p"/> And sealeth up the stars. ידעוּ ולא (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.9.5">Job 9:5</reference></hi>) may also be translated: without one’s perceiving it or knowing why; but it is more natural to take the mountains as the subject. אשׁר, <hi type="italic">quod</hi>, that (not “as,” Ewald, §333, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), after ידע, as <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.26">Eze 20:26</reference>; Ecc 8:12. Even the lofty mountains are quite unconscious of the change which He effects on them in a moment. Before they are aware that it is being done, it is over, as the <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. implies; the destructive power of His anger is irresistible, and effects its purpose suddenly. He causes the earth to start up from its place (comp. <reference osisRef="Isa.13.13">Isa 13:13</reference>) which it occupies in space (<reference osisRef="Job.26.7">Job 26:7</reference>); and by being thus set in motion by Him, its pillars tremble, i.e., its internal foundations (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.5">Psa 104:5</reference>), which are removed from human perception (<reference osisRef="Job.38.6">Job 38:6</reference>). It is not the highest mountains, which are rather called the pillars, as it were the supports, of heaven (<reference osisRef="Job.26.11">Job 26:11</reference>), that are meant. By the same almighty will He disposes of the sun and stars. The sun is here called חרס (as in Jdg 14:18 חרסה with unaccented <hi type="italic">ah</hi>, and as <reference osisRef="Isa.19.18">Isa 19:18</reference> <hi type="italic">‛Ir ha - Heres</hi> is a play upon החרס עיר, Ἡλιούπολις), perhaps from the same root as חרוּץ, one of the poetical names of gold. At His command the sun rises not, and He seals up the stars, i.e., conceals them behind thick clouds, so that the day becomes dark, and the night is not made bright. One may with Schultens think of the Flood, or with Warburton of the Egyptian darkness, and the standing still of the sun at the word of Joshua; but these are only single historical instances of a fact here affirmed as a universal experience of the divine power.
entries.aad5ff35cfb1f2f49e1b16b04a59dcfe542f62ff: <reference osisRef="Job.9.8-Job.10.8">Job 9:8-10   8</reference>  Who alone spreadeth out the heavens, <div eID="gen7182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7183" type="x-p"/> And walketh upon the heights of the sea;   9  Who made the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades, <div eID="gen7183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7184" type="x-p"/> And the chambers of the south; 10  Who doeth great things past finding out, <div eID="gen7184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7185" type="x-p"/> And wondrous things without number. <div eID="gen7185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7186" type="x-p"/> Ewald, Hirzel, and others, understand נטה (<reference osisRef="Job.9.8">Job 9:8</reference>) according to <reference osisRef="Ps.18.10">Psa 18:10</reference> : He letteth down the clouds of heaven, and walketh on the heights of the sea of clouds, i.e., high above the towering thunder-clouds. But parallel passages, such as <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Isa 40:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference>, and especially <reference osisRef="Isa.44.24">Isa 44:24</reference>, show that <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.9.8">Job 9:8</reference></hi> is to be understood as referring to the creation of the firmament of heaven; and consequently נטה is to be taken in the sense of <hi type="italic">expandere</hi>, and is a form of expression naturally occurring in connection with the mention of the waters which are separated by means of the רקיע. The question arises, whether ים here means the sea of waters above the firmament or upon the earth. According to the idea of the ancients, the waters which descend as rain have their habitation far away in the infinite expanse of the sky; the ocean of the sky (Egyptian <hi type="italic">Nun-pa</hi>), through which the sun-god <hi type="italic">Ra</hi> sails every day, is there. It is possible that ”the heights of the sea” here, and perhaps also “the roots of the sea” (<reference osisRef="Job.36.30">Job 36:30</reference>), may mean this ocean of the sky, as Hahn and Schlottmann suppose. But it is not necessary to adopt such an explanation, and it is moreover hazardous, since this conception of the celestial θάλασσα is not found elsewhere (apart from <reference osisRef="Rev.4.6">Rev 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.15.2">Rev 15:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.1">Rev 22:1</reference>). Why may not בּמתי, which is used of the heights of the clouds (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.14">Isa 14:14</reference>), be used also of the waves of the sea which mount up towards heaven (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.26">Psa 107:26</reference>)? God walks over them as man walks on level ground (lxx περιπατῶν ἐπὶ θαλάσσης ὡς ἐπ ̓ ἐδάφους); they rise or lie calmly beneath His feel according to His almighty will (comp. <reference osisRef="Hab.3.15">Hab 3:15</reference>). <div eID="gen7186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7187" type="x-p"/> Job next describes God as the Creator of the stars, by introducing a constellation of the northern (the Bear), one of the southern (Orion), and one of the eastern sky (the Pleiades). עשׁ, contracted from נעשׁ, Arabic <hi type="italic">na‛š</hi>, a bier, is the constellation of seven stars (<hi type="italic">septentrio </hi>or<hi type="italic">septentriones</hi>) in the northern sky. The Greater and the Lesser Bear form a square, which the Arabs regarded as a bier; the three other stars, <hi type="italic">benâth n‛asch ,</hi> i.e., daughters of the bier (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.38.32">Job 38:32</reference>), seem to be the mourners. כּסיל is Orion chained to the sky, which the ancients regarded as a powerful giant, and also as an insolent, foolish fellow<note placement="foot">The Arabic <hi type="italic">jâhil</hi> is similar, which combines the significations, an ignorant, foolhardy, and passionate man (vid., Fleischer, <hi type="italic">Ali’s hundert Sprûche</hi>, S. 115f.).</note> (K. O. Müller, <hi type="italic">Kleine deutsche Schriften,</hi> ii. 125). כּימה is the Pleiades, a constellation consisting of seven large and other smaller stars, Arabic <hi type="italic">turayyâ</hi>, which, like the Hebrew (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">kûmat , cumulus</hi>), signifies the heap, cluster (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.38.31">Job 38:31</reference>), and is compared by the Persian poets to a bouquet formed of jewels. It is the constellation of seven stars, whose rising and setting determined the commencement and end of their voyages (πλειάς, probably = constellation of navigation), and is to be distinguished from the northern <hi type="italic">septentriones</hi>. תּימן חדרי are, according to the Targ., the chambers of the constellations on the south side of the heavens, as also most expositors explain them (Mercier: <hi type="italic">sidera quae sunt in altero hemisphaerio versus alterum polum antarcticum</hi>), according to which תּימן, or written defectively תּמן, would therefore be equivalent to תמן כוכבי; or perhaps, in a more general meaning, the regions of the southern sky (<hi type="italic">penetralia</hi>), which are veiled, or altogether lost to view (Hirzel). In v. 10, Job says, almost <hi type="italic">verbatim</hi>, what Eliphaz had said (<reference osisRef="Job.5.10">Job 5:10</reference>). Job agrees with the friends in the recognition of the power of God, and intentionally describes those phases of it which display its terrible majesty. But while the friends deduce from this doctrine the duty of a humble deportment on the part of the sufferer, Job uses it to support the cheerless truth that human right can never be maintained in opposition to the absolute God.
entries.14629d7f6dc347a182131e6ce85d5aac95a878d4: Job 9:11-15 11  Behold, He goeth by me and I see not, <div eID="gen7187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7188" type="x-p"/> And passeth by and I perceive Him not. 12  Behold, He taketh away, who will hold Him back? <div eID="gen7188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7189" type="x-p"/> Who will say to Him: What doest Thou? 13  Eloah restraineth not His anger, <div eID="gen7189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7190" type="x-p"/> The helpers of Rahab stoop under Him - 14  How much less that I should address Him, <div eID="gen7190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7191" type="x-p"/> That I should choose the right words in answer to Him; 15  Because, though I were right, I could not answer, - <div eID="gen7191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7192" type="x-p"/> To Him as my Judge I must make supplication. <div eID="gen7192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7193" type="x-p"/> God works among men, as He works in nature, with a supreme control over all, invisibly, irresistibly, and is not responsible to any being (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Isa 45:9</reference>). He does not turn or restrain His anger without having accomplished His purpose. This is a proposition which, thus broadly expressed, is only partially true, as is evident from Psa 78:38. The helpers of <hi type="italic">Rahab</hi> must bow themselves under Him. It is not feasible to understand this in a general sense, as meaning those who are ready with boastful arrogance to yield succour to any against God. The form of expression which follows in <reference osisRef="Job.9.14">Job 9:14</reference>, “much less I,” supports the assumption that רהב עזרי refers to some well-known extraordinary example of wicked enterprise which had been frustrated, notwithstanding the gigantic strength by which it was supported; and שׁחהוּ may be translated by the present tense, since a familiar fact is used as synonymous with the expression of an universal truth. Elsewhere <hi type="italic">Rahab</hi> as a proper name denotes Egypt (<reference osisRef="Ps.87.4">Psa 87:4</reference>), but it cannot be so understood here, because direct references to events in the history of Israel are contrary to the character of the book, which, with remarkable consistency, avoids everything that is at all Israelitish. But how has Egypt obtained the name of <hi type="italic">Rahab?</hi> It is evident from <reference osisRef="Isa.30.7">Isa 30:7</reference> that it bears this name with reference to its deeds of prowess; but from <reference osisRef="Ps.89.11">Psa 89:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>, it is evident that <hi type="italic">Rahab</hi> properly denotes a sea-monster, which has become the symbol of Egypt, like <hi type="italic">tannîn</hi> and <hi type="italic">leviathan</hi> elsewhere. This signification of the word is also supported by <reference osisRef="Job.26.12">Job 26:12</reference>, where the lxx actually translate κητος, as here with remarkable freedom, ὑπ ̓ ἀυτοῦ ἐκάμφθησαν κήτη τὰ ὑπ ̓ οὐρανόν. It is not clear whether these ”sea-monsters” denote rebels cast down into the sea beneath the sky, or chained upon the sky; but at any rate the consciousness of a distinct mythological meaning in רהב עזרי is expressed by this translation (as also in the still freer translation of Jerome, <hi type="italic">et sub quo curvantur qui portant orbem</hi>); probably a myth connected with such names of the constellations as Κῆτος and Πρίστις (Ewald, Hirz., Schlottm.). The poesy of the book of Job even in other places does not spurn mythological allusions; and the phrase before us reminds one of the Hindu myth of <hi type="italic">Indras'</hi> victory over the dark demon <hi type="italic">Vritras</hi>, who tries to delay the descent of rain, and over his helpers. In <hi type="italic">Vritras</hi>, as in רהב, there is the idea of hostile resistance. <div eID="gen7193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7194" type="x-p"/> Job compares himself, the feeble one, to these mythical titanic powers in Job 9:14. כּי אף (properly: even that), or even אף alone (<reference osisRef="Job.4.19">Job 4:19</reference>), signifies, according as the connection introduces a climax or anti-climax, either <hi type="italic">quanto magis </hi>or <hi type="italic">quanto minus,</hi> as here: how much less can I, the feeble one, dispute with Him! אשׁר, <reference osisRef="Job.9.15">Job 9:15</reference>, is best taken, as in <reference osisRef="Job.5.5">Job 5:5</reference>, in the signification <hi type="italic">quoniam</hi>. The <hi type="italic">part. Poel</hi> משׁפטי we should more correctly translate “my disputant” than “my judge;” it is Poel which Ewald appropriately styles the conjugation of attack: שׁופט, <hi type="italic">judicando vel litigando aliquem petere; comp. </hi> Ges. §55, 1. The <hi type="italic">part. Kal</hi> denotes a judge, the <hi type="italic">part. Poel</hi> one who is accuser and judge at the same time. On such Poel-forms from strong roots, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.109.10">Psa 109:10</reference>, where <hi type="italic">wedorschu</hi> is to be read, and therefore it is written ודרשׁוּ in correct Codices.
entries.0eddb637b6177532b20594271059d7abb8bc00a5: Job 9:16-20 16  If when I called He really answered, <div eID="gen7194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7195" type="x-p"/> I could not believe that He would hearken to me; 17  He would rather crush me in a tempest, <div eID="gen7195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7196" type="x-p"/> And only multiply my wounds without cause; 18  He would not suffer me to take my breath, <div eID="gen7196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7197" type="x-p"/> But would fill me with bitter things. 19  If it is a question of the strength of the strong - : “Behold here!” <div eID="gen7197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7198" type="x-p"/> And if of right - : “Who will challenge me?” 20  Where I in the right, my mouth must condemn me; <div eID="gen7198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7199" type="x-p"/> Were I innocent, He would declare me guilty. <div eID="gen7199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7200" type="x-p"/> The answer of God when called upon, i.e., summoned, is represented in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.9.16">Job 9:16</reference></hi> as an actual result (<hi type="italic">praet</hi>. followed by <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi>), therefore <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.9.16">Job 9:16</reference></hi> cannot be intended to express: I could not believe that He answers me, but: I could not believe that He, the answerer, would hearken to me; His infinite exaltation would not permit such condescension. The אשׁר which follows, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.9.17">Job 9:17</reference></hi>, signifies either <hi type="italic">quippe qui</hi> or <hi type="italic">quoniam</hi>; both shades of meaning are after all blended, as in Job 9:15. The question arises here whether שׁוף signifies <hi type="italic">conterere</hi>, or as cognate form with שׁאף, <hi type="italic">inhiare</hi>, - a question also of importance in the exposition of the <hi type="italic">Protevangelium</hi>. There are in all only three passages in which it occurs: here, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen 3:15</reference>, and Psa 139:11. In <reference osisRef="Ps.139.11">Psa 139:11</reference> the meaning <hi type="italic">conterere</hi> is unsuitable, but even the signification <hi type="italic">inhiare</hi> can only be adopted for want of a better: perhaps it may be explained by comparison with צעף, in the sense of <hi type="italic">obvelare</hi>, or as a denominative from נשׁף (the verb of which, נשׁף, is kindred to נשׁב, נשׁם, <hi type="italic">flare</hi>) in the signification <hi type="italic">obtenebrare</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen 3:15</reference>, if regarded superficially, the meaning <hi type="italic">inhiare</hi> and <hi type="italic">conterere</hi> are alike suitable, but the meaning <hi type="italic">inhiare</hi> deprives that utterance of God of its prophetic character, which has been recognised from the beginning; and the meaning <hi type="italic">conterere</hi>, <hi type="italic">contundere</hi>, is strongly supported by the translations. We decide in favour of this meaning also in the present passage, with the ancient translations (lxx ἐκτρίψῃ, Targ. מדקדּק, <hi type="italic">comminuens</hi>). Moreover, it is the meaning most generally supported by a comparison with the dialects, whereas the signification <hi type="italic">inhiare</hi> can only be sustained by comparison with שׁאף and the Arabic <hi type="italic">sâfa</hi> (to sniff, track by scent, to smell); besides, “to assail angrily” (Hirz., Ewald) is an inadmissible contortion of <hi type="italic">inhiare</hi>, which signifies in a hostile sense “to seize abruptly” (Schlottm.), properly to snatch, to desire to seize. <div eID="gen7200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7201" type="x-p"/> Translate therefore: He would crush me in a tempest and multiply (<hi type="italic">multiplicaret</hi>), etc., would not let me take breath (<hi type="italic">respirare</hi>), but (כּי, Ges. §155, 1, <hi type="italic">e</hi>. <hi type="italic">a</hi>.) fill me (ישׂבּיענּי, with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> with <hi type="italic">Rebia mugrasch</hi>) with bitter things (ממּררים, with <hi type="italic">Dag</hi>. <hi type="italic">dirimens</hi>, which gives the word a more pathetic expression). The meaning of <reference osisRef="Job.9.19">Job 9:19</reference> is that God stifles the attempt to maintain one’s right in the very beginning by His being superior to the creature in strength, and not entering into a dispute with him concerning the right. הנּה (for הנּני as איּה, <reference osisRef="Job.15.23">Job 15:23</reference>, for איּו): see, here I am, ready for the contest, is the word of God, similar to <hi type="italic">quis citare possit me</hi> (in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.19">Jer 49:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.44">Jer 50:44</reference>), which sounds as an echo of this passage. The creature must always be in the wrong, - a thought true in itself, in connection with which Job forgets that God’s right in opposition to the creature is also always the true objective right. פּי, with suffix, accented to indicate its logical connection, as <reference osisRef="Job.15.6">Job 15:6</reference> : my own mouth.<note placement="foot">Olshausen’s conjecture, פּיו, lessens the difficulty in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.16">Isa 34:16</reference>, but here it destroys the strong expression of the violence done to the moral consciousness.</note> <div eID="gen7201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7202" type="x-p"/> In ויּעקשׁני the <hi type="italic">Chirek</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> is shortened to a <hi type="italic">Sheva</hi>, as <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.25">1Sa 17:25</reference>; vid., Ges. §53, rem. 4. The subject is God, not “my mouth” (Schlottm.): supposing that I were innocent, He would put me down as one morally wrong and to be rejected.
entries.81d5a39d74ef1ffa85819864a19a5be09f12f426: Job 9:21-24 21  Whether I am innocent, I know not myself, <div eID="gen7202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7203" type="x-p"/> My life is offensive to me. 22  There is one thing-therefore I maintain - : <div eID="gen7203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7204" type="x-p"/> The innocent and wicked He destroyeth. 23  If the scourge slay suddenly, <div eID="gen7204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7205" type="x-p"/> He laugheth at the melting away of the innocent. 24  Countries are given into the hand of the wicked; <div eID="gen7205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7206" type="x-p"/> The countenance of its rulers He veileth - <div eID="gen7206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7207" type="x-p"/> Is it not so, who else doeth it? <div eID="gen7207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7208" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.9.21">Job 9:21</reference> is usually considered to be an affirmation of innocence on the part of Job, though without effect, and even at the peril of his own destruction: ”I am innocent, I boldly say it even with scorn of my life” (Schnurr., Hirz., Ewald, Schlottm.). But although נפשׁי אדע לא may mean: I care nothing for my soul, i.e., my life (comp. <reference osisRef="Gen.39.6">Gen 39:6</reference>), its first meaning would be: I know not my soul, i.e., myself; and this sense is also quite in accordance with the context. He is innocent, but the contradiction between his lot and his innocence seems to show that his self-consciousness is deceptive, and makes him a mystery to himself, leads him astray respecting himself; and having thus become a stranger to himself, he abhors this life of seeming contradictions, for which he desires nothing less than its long continuance (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.7.16">Job 7:16</reference>). The היא אחת which follows we do not explain: “it is all the same to me whether I live or not,” but: it is all one whether man is innocent or not. He himself is a proof of this; therefore he maintains, etc. It is, however, also possible that this expression, which is similar in meaning to <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.2">Ecc 9:2</reference> (there is one event, אחד מקרה, to the righteous and to the wicked), and is well translated in the Targ. by היא מכילא חדא (there is one measure of retribution, מכילא = מדּה, μέτρον, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.2">Mat 7:2</reference>), refers to what follows, and that “therefore I maintain” is parenthetical (like אמרתי, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.57">Psa 119:57</reference>; אמר לי, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Isa 45:24</reference>), and we have translated it accordingly. There is certainly a kind of suspense, and על־כן d introduces an assertion of Job, which is founded upon the fact of the continuance of his own misfortune, - an assertion which he advances in direct contradiction to the friends, and which is expressly censured by Elihu. <div eID="gen7208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7209" type="x-p"/> In Job 9:23., by some striking examples, he completes the description of that which seems to be supported by the conflict he is called to endure. שׁוט, a scourge, signifies a judgment which passes over a nation (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.15">Isa 28:15</reference>). It swept off the guiltless as well, and therefore Job concludes that God delights in מסּה, πειρασμός, trial, or perhaps more correctly the melting away (from מסס, as <reference osisRef="Job.6.14">Job 6:14</reference>) of the guiltless, i.e., their dissolution in anguish and dismay, their wearing away and despondency. Jerome rightly remarks that in the whole book Job says <hi type="italic">nihil asperius</hi> than what he says in Job 9:23. Another example in favour of his disconsolate היא אחת is that whole lands are given into the hand of the wicked: the monarch is an evil man, and the countenance of their judges He (God) covers, so that they do not distinguish between right and wrong, nor decide in favour of the former rather than of the latter. God himself is the final cause of the whole: if not, i.e., if it is not so, who can it then be that causes it? אפו (four times in the book of Job instead of the usual form אפוא) is, according to the current opinion, placed <hi type="italic">per hyperbaton</hi> in the conditional instead of the interrogative clause; and מי אפו are certainly not, with Hirzel, to be taken together. There is, however, not a proper <hi type="italic">hyperbaton</hi>, but אפו here gives intensity to the question; though not directly as <reference osisRef="Job.17.15">Job 17:15</reference> (Ges. §153, 2), but only indirectly, by giving intensity to that which introduces the question, as <reference osisRef="Job.24.25">Job 24:25</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gen.27.37">Gen 27:37</reference>; translate therefore: if it really is not so (comp. the Homeric expression ει ̓ δ ̓ ἄγε). It is indisputable that God, and no one else, is the final cause of this misery, apparently so full of contradiction, which meets us in the history of mankind, and which Job now experiences for himself.
entries.a01d84725bd9980dfd6a0356c9d87f7308cefc75: Job 9:25-28 25  My days were swifter than a runner, <div eID="gen7209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7210" type="x-p"/> They fled away without seeing prosperity, 26  They shot by as ships of reeds, <div eID="gen7210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7211" type="x-p"/> As an eagle which dasheth upon its prey. 27  If my thought is: I will forget my complaint, <div eID="gen7211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7212" type="x-p"/> I will give up my dark looks and look cheerful; 28  I shudder at all my pains, <div eID="gen7212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7213" type="x-p"/> I feel that Thou dost not pronounce me innocent. <div eID="gen7213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7214" type="x-p"/> Such, as described in the preceding strophe, is the lot of the innocent in general, and such (this is the connection) is also Job’s lot: his swiftly passing life comes to an end amidst suffering, as that of an evil-doer whom God cuts off in judgment. In the midst of his present sufferings he has entirely forgotten his former prosperity; it is no happiness to him, because the very enjoyment of it makes the loss of it more grievous to bear. The days of prosperity are gone, have passed swiftly away without טובה, i.e., without <hi type="italic">lasting</hi> prosperity. They have been swifter רץ מנּי. By reference to <reference osisRef="Job.7.6">Job 7:6</reference>, this might be considered as a figure borrowed from the weaver’s loom, since in the Coptic the threads of the weft (<hi type="italic">fila subteminis</hi>) which are wound round the shuttle are called ”runners” (vid., Ges. <hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi>); but Rosenmüller has correctly observed that, in order to describe the fleetness of his life, Job brings together that which is swiftest on land (the runners or couriers), in water (fast-sailing ships), and in the air (the swooping eagle). עם, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.9.26">Job 9:26</reference></hi>, signifies, in comparison with, <hi type="italic">aeque ac.</hi> But we possess only a rather uncertain tradition as to the kind of vessels meant by אבה אניות. Jerome translates, after the Targ.: <hi type="italic">naves poma portantes</hi>, by which one may understand the small vessels, according to Edrisi, common on the Dead Sea, in which corn and different kinds of fruits were carried from Zoar to Jericho and to other regions of the Jordan (Stickel, S. 267); but if אבה were connected with אב, we might rather expect אבּה, after the form אשּׁה (from אשׁ), instead of אבה. Others derive the word from אבה, <hi type="italic">avere</hi>: ships of desire, i.e., full-rigged and ready for sea (Gecatilia in Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes. suppl.</hi> p. 62), or struggling towards the goal (Kimchi), or steering towards (Zamora), and consequently hastening to (Symmachuc, σπευδούσαις), the harbour; but independently of the explanation not being suited to the description, it should then be accented <hi type="italic">êbeh</hi>, after the form נדה, קצה, instead of <hi type="italic">êbéh</hi>. The explanation, ships of hostility (Syr.),<note placement="foot">Luther also perhaps understood pirate ships, when he translated, “<hi type="italic">wie die starcken Schiff</hi>.”</note> i.e., ships belonging to pirates or freebooters, privateers, which would suit the subject well, is still less admissible with the present pointing of the text, as it must then be אבה (איבה), with which the Egyptian <hi type="italic">uba</hi>, against, and adverse (<hi type="italic">contrarius</hi>), may be compared. According to Abulwalid (Parchon, Raschi), אבה is the name of a large river near the scene of the book of Job; which may be understood as either the Babylonian name for river Arab. <hi type="italic">'bby</hi>, or the Abyssinian name of the Nile, <hi type="italic">abâï</hi>; and אבה may be compared with לבנה in relation to the Arabic, <hi type="italic">lubna</hi>. But a far more satisfactory explanation is the one now generally received, according to the comparison with the Arabic <hi type="italic">abâ'un</hi>, a reed (whence <hi type="italic">abaa - t - un</hi>, a reed, a so-called <hi type="italic">n. unitatis</hi>): ships made from reeds, like גּמא כּלי, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Isa 18:2</reference>, vessels of papyrus, βαρίδες παπύριναι. In such small ships, with Egyptian tackling, they used to travel as far as Taprobane. These canoes were made to fold together, <hi type="italic">plicatiles</hi>, so that they could be carried past the cataracts; Heliodorus describes them as ὀξυδρομώτατα.<note placement="foot">There is no Egyptian word which can be compared to אבה, whereas <hi type="italic">han</hi> (<hi type="italic">hani</hi>) or <hi type="italic">an</hi> (<hi type="italic">ana</hi>) in Egyptian, like the Hebrew אניה, means a ship (vid., Chabas, <hi type="italic">Le Papyrus magique Harris</hi>, p. 246, No. 826, cf. pp. 33, 47); it is written with the sign for set = downwards, since they fastened a stone at the front of the vessel, as was even known to Herodotus, in order to accelerate its speed in descending the river. From this one might conjecture for the passage before us אבן אניות = swift sailers.</note> <div eID="gen7214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7215" type="x-p"/> The third figure is the eagle, which swoops down upon its prey; טוּשׂ, like Chaldee טוּס, by which the Targ. translates השׁ, <reference osisRef="Hab.1.8">Hab 1:8</reference>; Grätz' conjecture of ישׁוּט (which is intended to mean flutters) is superfluous. Just as unnecessary is it, with Olshausen, to change אמרי אם into אמרתי אם: “if my saying (thinking)” is equivalent to, “as often as I say (think).” פנים is here (as in the German phrase, <hi type="italic">ein Gesicht machen</hi>) an ill-humoured, distorted, wry face. When Job desires to give up this look of suffering and be cheerful (הבליג, like <reference osisRef="Job.10.20">Job 10:20</reference>, <hi type="italic">hilaritatem prae se ferre, vultum hilarem induere</hi>), the certainty that he is not favoured of God, and consequently that he cannot be delivered from his sufferings, all his anguish in spite of his struggles against it comes ever afresh before his mind. It is scarcely necessary to remark that תנקני is addressed to God, not to Bildad. It is important to notice that Job does not speak of God without at the same time looking up to Him as in prayer. Although he feels rejected of God, he still remains true to God. In the following strophe he continues to complain of God, but without denying Him.
entries.f1489939502048fc33a5de0070353a7fb71e244f: Job 9:29-33 29  If I am wicked, why do I exert myself in vain? 30  If I should wash myself with snow water, <div eID="gen7215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7216" type="x-p"/> And make my hands clean with lye, 31  Then thou wouldst plunge me into the pit, <div eID="gen7216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7217" type="x-p"/> And my clothes would abhor me. 32  For He is not a man as I, that I should answer Him, <div eID="gen7217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7218" type="x-p"/> That we should go together to judgment. 33  There is not an arbitrator between us <div eID="gen7218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7219" type="x-p"/> Who should lay his hand upon us both. <div eID="gen7219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7220" type="x-p"/> The clause with strongly accented “I” affirms that in relation to God is from the first, and unchangeably, a wicked, i.e., guilty, man (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.7">Psa 109:7</reference>) (רשׁע, to be a wicked man, means either to act as such <reference osisRef="Job.10.15">Job 10:15</reference>, or to appear as such, be accounted as such, as here and <reference osisRef="Job.10.7">Job 10:7</reference>; <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>., <reference osisRef="Job.9.20">Job 9:20</reference>, to condemn). Why, therefore, should he vainly (הבל, <hi type="italic">acc. adv.,</hi> like breath, useless) exert himself by crying for help, and basing his plaint on his innocence? In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.9.30">Job 9:30</reference></hi> the <hi type="italic">Chethib</hi> is במו, the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> במי, as the reverse in <reference osisRef="Isa.25.10">Isa 25:10</reference>; <hi type="italic">mo</hi> itself appears in the signification water (Egyptian <hi type="italic">muau</hi>), in the proper names <hi type="italic">Moab</hi> and <hi type="italic">Moshe</hi> (according to Jablonsky, <hi type="italic">ex aqua servatus</hi>); in במו, however, the <hi type="italic">mo</hi> may be understood according to Ges. §103, 2. This is the meaning - no cleansing, even though he should use snow and בּר (a vegetable alkali), i.e., not even the best-grounded self-justification can avail him, for God would still bring it to pass, that his clearly proved innocence should change to the most horrible impurity. Ewald, Rödiger, and others translate incorrectly: my clothes would make me disgusting. The idea is tame. The <hi type="italic">Piel</hi> תּעב signifies elsewhere in the book (<reference osisRef="Job.19.19">Job 19:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.30.10">Job 30:10</reference>) to abhor, not to make abhorrent; and the causative meaning is indeed questionable, for מתעב (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.7">Isa 49:7</reference>) signifies loathing, as מכסּה (<reference osisRef="Job.23.17">Job 23:17</reference>) covering, and <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.25">Eze 16:25</reference> certainly borders on the signification “to make detestable,” but תעב may also be in the primary meaning, <hi type="italic">abominari</hi>, the strongest expression for that contempt of the beauty bestowed by God which manifests itself by prostitution. Translate: My clothes would abhor me; which does not mean: I should be disgusted with myself (Hirzel); Job is rather represented as naked; him, the naked one, God would - says he - so plunge into the pit that his clothes would conceive a horror of him, i.e., start back in terror at the idea of being put on and defiled by such a horrible creature (Schlottm., Oehler). For God is not his equal, standing on the same level with him: He, the Absolute Being, is accuser and judge in one person; there is between them no arbitrator who (or that he) should lay, etc. Mercier correctly explains: <hi type="italic">impositio manus est potestatis signum; the meaning therefore is: qui utrumque nostrum velut manu imposita coerceat.  </hi>
entries.3aadbb1896369aa8ff43ed282a12f63bbcb3b4ef: Job 9:34-35 34  Let Him take away His rod from me, <div eID="gen7220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7221" type="x-p"/> And let His terrors not stupify me. 35  Then I would speak and not fear Him, <div eID="gen7221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7222" type="x-p"/> For not thus do I stand with myself. <div eID="gen7222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7223" type="x-p"/> The two Optatives, Job 9:34., as is frequently the case with the Imper., are followed by the Cohortative as the conclusion (אדבּרה, therefore will I speak; whereas ואדברה might be equivalent to, in order that I may speak) of a conditional antecedent clause. שׁבט is here the rod with which God smites Job; comp. Job 13:21. If God would only remove his pain from him for a brief space, so that he might recover himself for self-defence, and if He would not stifle his words as they come freely forth from his lips by confronting him with His overwhelming majesty, then he would fearlessly express himself; for “not thus am I in myself,” i.e., I am not conscious of such a moral condition as compels me to remain dumb before Him. However, we must inquire whether, according to the context, this special reference and shade of meaning is to be given to לא־כן. There is a use of כן = nothing, when accompanied by a gesture expressive of contemptuous rejection, Num 13:33 (כמו־כן, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.6">Isa 51:6</reference>, as nothing);<note placement="foot">In both these passages (to which Böttcher adds <reference osisRef="Ps.127.2">Psa 127:2</reference>, “so = without anything further”), כּן has been considered to be the sing. of כּנּים, gnats; but this sing. is an error, as בּיץ, formerly considered to be the sing. of בּיצים. The respective sing. are כּנּה, בּיצה.</note> and a use of לא־כן = not only so = not so small, so useless, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.5">2Sa 23:5</reference>, accompanied by a gesture expressive of the denial of such contempt, according to which the present passage may probably be explained: I am in myself, i.e., according to the testimony of my conscience, not so, i.e., not so morally worthless and devoid of right.<hi type="italic"></hi>  <chapter eID="Job.9"/> <div eID="gen7223" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="32">32. For <ns0:hi>he is</ns0:hi> not a man as <ns0:hi>I am</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">But one infinitely superiour to me in Majesty, and Power, and Wisdom, and Justice.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> I should an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swer him <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That I should presume to debate my cause with him, or answer his allegations against me.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and that</ns0:hi> we should come together <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Face to face, to plead upon equal terms before a superiour and indifferent Judge.</ns0:note> in Judg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Sam. 2. 25. ver. 19.</ns0:note> Neither is there <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> one that shall argue.</ns0:note> any <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> Umpire.</ns0:note> days<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>man <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>a Reprover;</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>a Judge</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Umpire,</ns0:hi> whose office was to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />prove the guilty person.</ns0:note> betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Use his power and authority to appoint the time and place of our meeting; to order and govern us in pleading; and to oblige us to stand to his decision. The <ns0:hi>hand</ns0:hi> is oft put for <ns0:hi>power,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>laying on the hand</ns0:hi> upon another was oft-times an act and sign of superiority and dominion.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="34">34. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13. 21. & 33. 7.</ns0:note> Let him take his Rod away from me, and let not his fear <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Objectively so called, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The fear and dread of him, of his Majesty and justice. Let him not deal with me rigorously accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to his soveraign dominion and perfect justice, but according to his wonted grace and clemency.</ns0:note> terrifie me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="35">35. <ns0:hi>Then</ns0:hi> would I speak, and not fear him, <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I would speak freely for my self, being freed from the dread of his Majesty, which takes away my spirit and courage, and stoppeth my mouth.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> But I am not so with my self.</ns0:note> but <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> not so with me <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> I am not free from his terrour, and therefore cannot and dare not plead my cause boldly with him; and so have nothing else to do but to ease my self by receiving my complaints, as he doth in the next words. Oth. thus, <ns0:hi>But I am not so with my self, i. e.</ns0:hi> I am in a manner besides my self, distracted with the terrours of God upon me. Or rather thus, <ns0:hi>For I am not s<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> with my self,</ns0:hi> or in my own Conscience, as I perceive I am in your eyes; to wit, an Hypocrite and ungodly man. So this is a reason why he could speak to God without slavish fear, because he was conscious to himself of his own Integrity: I have a good Conscience within my self, and therefore could use boldness in speaking to God, provided he would not deal with me in strict justice, but upon the terms of grace and mercy which he hath proposed to sinners, and with allowance to humane Infir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
